source: Rescorla (SEP) The Language of Thought Hypothesis
finding: LOTH says thinking happens in a mental language (Mentalese) whose complex symbols are built from primitive symbols by rules. It rests on the Representational Theory of Thought: believing p means bearing a relation to a mental representation S that means p.
numbers: Core theses listed: RTT, compositionality (COMP), logical structure (LOGIC), classical computation (CCTM), formal syntactic computation (FSC).
quote: X believes that p iff there is a mental representation S such that X believes* S and S means that p.
limits: All arguments for LOTH are abductive (inference to best explanation). Semantic computationalists reject FSC.
agent_relevance: Background only. The scaffold already treats thought as structured steps run by code; LOTH gives the vocabulary but adds no operator.

source: Rescorla (SEP) productivity argument
finding: Productivity argument: a finite thinker can entertain unboundedly many thoughts. A finite stock of primitive symbols plus recursive combination rules explains this.
numbers: No numbers. Argument is a-priori plus competence idealisation.
limits: Real thinkers are bounded by memory and time, so productivity is a competence claim, not a performance fact. SEP notes establishing it for perception or navigation does not show it for high-level thought.
agent_relevance: Gives a test shape for LLMs: does performance hold as length or depth grows beyond training (Lake-Baroni length split, Hupkes productivity).

source: Rescorla (SEP) systematicity of thought and of thinking
finding: Systematicity of thought: whoever can think John loves Mary can think Mary loves John. Systematicity of inference: whoever infers p from p-and-q can infer m from m-and-n. Compositional symbols and one uniform syntactic operation explain both.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Fodor treats it as a nomic regularity; critics question how systematic real cognition is. Only partly checked here.
agent_relevance: Systematicity is the property to test in LLMs: recombining known parts into new wholes (SCAN, COGS, CFQ).

source: Fodor and Pylyshyn (1988) critique of connectionism, as reconstructed in SEP
finding: Fodor and Pylyshyn argue systematicity and productivity must be explained by any cognitive theory and only classical (symbols with constituent structure) architectures explain them. Eliminative connectionism has no built-in guarantee of systematicity; implementationist connectionism survives.
numbers: Argument, no data. Reconstructed by Aydede in SEP.
quote: nothing about the connectionist framework per se guarantees systematicity
limits: Read via SEP, not the 1988 paper itself (the PDF was not reachable). Core claim is that nothing guarantees systematicity in the framework, not that nets cannot do it.
agent_relevance: Frames the modern LLM debate: the question is whether a net trained by gradient descent acquires systematicity, not whether it can in principle.

source: Rescorla (SEP) replies: Smolensky, Chalmers, van Gelder; Fodor-McLaughlin 1990
finding: Replies reject the premise that structured representation needs concatenative constituency. Smolensky, Chalmers and van Gelder use distributed vectors with implicit constituency via tensor operations. Fodor and McLaughlin (1990) answer that such constituents are not causally present, so they cannot explain systematicity. Chalmers (1993) and Niklasson-van Gelder (1994) show nets can do structure-sensitive transformations.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Dispute is about whether implicit vector structure counts as constituency; never settled by data in the SEP text.
agent_relevance: Same fork appears for LLMs: hidden-state structure may carry composition without explicit symbols; only behaviour tests are available to us.

source: Gallistel and King (2009) as summarised in SEP; Tolman cognitive maps
finding: Gallistel and King defend COMP+CCTM+FSC mainly with non-human cases (navigation, memory) and say these show productivity that classical computation explains and eliminative connectionism does not. SEP reports broad consensus that mammals, perhaps some insects, navigate with represented spatial layout.
numbers: No numbers in the SEP text.
limits: Book itself not opened. SEP warns perception and navigation evidence does not establish RTT for high-level human thought.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Lake and Baroni (2018) Generalization without systematicity (SCAN), experiment 1 random split
finding: Seq2seq nets trained on SCAN commands generalise well to a random held-out 20 percent, and to sparse coverage. This shows mix-and-match generalisation works when test items are near training items.
numbers: Best net (LSTM, 2x200, no attention) 99.8% on test, best-overall 99.7%; classic simple RNN under 1.5%; attention SRN 59.7% mean (range 18.4-94.0%). Training on 1% of commands (~210 examples) ~5%; 2% ~54%; 4% ~93%. Averages of 5 runs; 100k training presentations.
limits: Test items mostly share every sub-command with training (avg 8 occurrences at 2% coverage).
agent_relevance: Random-split success is not evidence of systematicity; use compositional splits when auditing.

source: Lake and Baroni (2018) SCAN experiment 2 length split
finding: Training on action sequences up to 22 steps and testing on longer ones (up to 48) is very hard. This is the productivity test and nets fail.
numbers: Top-by-split model (GRU+attention, 1x50, dropout 0.5) 20.8% mean over 5 runs; overall-best 13.8%. Oracle length at test raised these to 60.2% and 23.6%. Even top model fell from 95.76% for 24-action commands to 22.8% for 48 actions. Search failures under 1 command per thousand.
limits: Oracle helps but does not fix it. Later work (Csordas 2021) shows part is the end-of-sequence decision.
agent_relevance: Length extrapolation is a known weak spot; the scaffold should not rely on a model emitting long unaided derivations.

source: Lake and Baroni (2018) SCAN experiment 3 add-jump and turn-left
finding: The dax thought experiment made real: if a net learns a new primitive only in isolation, it cannot use it in composed commands. The contrast between jump and turn left shows success depends on whether the primitive's action was seen in composition.
numbers: Turn left: best 90.3% (GRU+attention), overall-best 90.0%. Jump: best 1.2% (LSTM+attention), overall-best 0.08%. With jump shown in 8 composed commands 38.3%; 16 commands 77.8%; 32 commands 88.4%. Primitive over-sampled to 10% of presentations.
quote: if you know the meaning of 'run', 'jump' and 'run twice', you should also understand what 'jump twice' means.
limits: All 45 errors of the best turn-left model were conjunctions containing turn left, so even good performance came in a non-systematic way.
agent_relevance: A newly defined term must be exercised in several composed contexts before use; relevant to in-context definitions in the scaffold.

source: Keysers et al. (2020) Measuring compositional generalization (CFQ, DBCA)
finding: Introduces CFQ (question to SPARQL) and a method that maximises compound divergence while keeping atom divergence low. Accuracy falls as compound divergence rises, across three architectures and also on SCAN.
numbers: CFQ random split: LSTM+attn 97.4, Transformer 98.5, Universal Transformer 98.0. MCD splits: 14.9, 17.9, 18.9. SCAN random 99.9/100.0/99.9; SCAN MCD 6.1, 1.1, 1.2 (percent, 5 runs).
limits: Baselines trained from scratch, not pretrained LLMs. Later pretrained models do much better on CFQ (not verified here).
agent_relevance: Gives a quantitative lever: compositional difficulty is a measurable divergence of recombined compounds, useful for building our own held-out tests.

source: Kim and Linzen (2020) COGS
finding: COGS tests lexical and structural generalisation in semantic parsing. In-distribution accuracy is near perfect, generalisation poor and seed-sensitive. Structural cases (PP modifier on subject, deeper embedding) are near zero.
numbers: In-distribution 96-99%; generalisation 16-35% with seed sd about 6-8 points. Bidirectional LSTM 0.16 (sd 0.08), unidirectional LSTM 0.32 (sd 0.06). PP depth generalisation: LSTM 2%, BiLSTM and Transformer near 0%. Active-to-passive Transformer near 100%.
limits: Models trained from scratch with no pretraining; 5 seeds.
agent_relevance: Structure-novel inputs are where failure concentrates; word-novel inputs are easier.

source: Hupkes et al. (2020) Compositionality decomposed (PCFG SET, five tests)
finding: Splits compositionality into five testable facets: systematicity, productivity, substitutivity, localism, overgeneralisation, and tests LSTM, ConvS2S and Transformer on a PCFG string-edit task.
numbers: In-distribution accuracy: LSTMS2S 0.79, ConvS2S 0.85, Transformer 0.92. Systematicity drops 33%, 34%, 22% relative to task accuracy. Productivity with long sequences removed from training: Transformer 0.50, LSTM 0.30, ConvS2S 0.31 (drops 46%, 62%, 64%). Substitutivity consistency reported 0.60 / 0.58 / 0.90 for LSTM / ConvS2S / Transformer.
limits: Small models on synthetic data; authors warn results are not general claims about each architecture. Table alignment in text extraction was ambiguous for some consistency scores.
agent_relevance: Use this five-way split to name which kind of generalisation a scaffold check is probing.

source: Csordas, Irie, Schmidhuber (2021) The devil is in the detail
finding: Much SCAN-style failure of Transformers was due to training details (embedding scaling, early stopping on IID validation, relative positions, Universal Transformer). Fixing them greatly improves systematic generalisation without symbolic parts.
numbers: PCFG productivity 50% to 85%; COGS 35% to 81%; SCAN length split 100% with relative positional embedding; also improved CFQ and Mathematics dataset.
limits: Still tied to specific datasets; early stopping on an in-distribution validation set misleads about generalisation.
agent_relevance: Failed systematicity results can be partly engineering artefacts; treat a single failing benchmark as weak evidence about no-symbols.

source: Zhou et al. (2022) Least-to-most prompting
finding: Prompting code-davinci-002 to first decompose a command and then solve sub-commands solves SCAN including the length split, with 14 exemplars. Prior neural-symbolic systems also reached 100% but needed specialised training.
numbers: SCAN length split: standard prompting 16.7%, chain-of-thought 16.2%, least-to-most 99.7%. Same solve rate on other splits and full SCAN. 13 failures in the length-split test set.
limits: Prompts encode the SCAN grammar structure (decomposition and mapping prompts); a pretrained LLM plus explicit decomposition, not zero-shot systematicity.
agent_relevance: Strong support for our design: a prompt or program that imposes decomposition and recombination gives the systematic behaviour the bare model lacks.

source: Lake and Baroni (2023) Human-like systematic generalization through meta-learning (MLC)
finding: Meta-learning for compositionality (MLC) trains a small transformer on a stream of episodes, so it learns systematicity as a skill. It matches human few-shot performance on a pseudolanguage task and solves SCAN and COGS lexical splits.
numbers: Humans (n=25) exact algebraic output 80.7%; MLC 82.4%. Longer outputs: human 72.5%, MLC 77.8%. MLC reproduces one-to-one errors (56.3% of errors) and modal human response 65.0%. Error rates (5 runs): SCAN add jump 0.22% vs basic seq2seq 99.27%; around right 0.04% vs 51.13%; opposite right 0.06% vs 100%; COGS lexical 0.87% vs 6.08%. About 1.4M parameters, 3 encoder and 3 decoder layers.
limits: Read through the PMC copy. MLC fails SCAN length split and three COGS structural types (100% error). Authors say preliminary GPT-4 experiments (SI, not read) suggest systematicity is still open.
agent_relevance: Systematicity can be learned by training on tasks that demand it, but only for the kinds of recombination in the training episodes.

source: Dziri et al. (2023) Faith and Fate: limits of transformers on compositionality
finding: On multi-digit multiplication, logic grid puzzles and a DP task, transformer LLMs seem to reduce multi-step reasoning to matching linearised subgraphs seen in training, not to systematic procedures. Accuracy decays to near zero as computation-graph size grows.
numbers: 3-digit by 3-digit multiplication: ChatGPT 55%, GPT-4 59% (zero-shot). Zero-shot accuracy falls toward 0 with larger problem size. One analysis: 82.3% of correct 4-digit by 2-digit answers had restoration errors near zero (context partly unclear in extraction).
limits: Zero-shot, few-shot and finetuning of 2023 models; scratchpads help in-distribution only.
agent_relevance: Supports offloading exact multi-step computation to code, which is already a guardrail of our schema.

source: Berglund et al. (2023) The Reversal Curse
finding: LLMs finetuned on A is B fail to answer B is A. A direct failure of a symmetry generalisation that a structured symbolic store would satisfy.
numbers: GPT-3-175B: name given description in matched order 96.7% exact match; description given name in matched order 50.0%; reversed order close to 0%, no better than random names.
limits: Applies to finetuning and training data; in-context the reverse works (authors note, appendix B.6).
agent_relevance: Put needed facts in context in both directions; do not expect retrieval of the converse from weights.

source: Wu et al. (2023) Reasoning or Reciting: counterfactual task variants
finding: Across 11 tasks (base-9 arithmetic, code with 1-based indexing, chess variants, spatial tasks, SET and others) models beat chance on counterfactual variants but performance falls substantially and consistently relative to default. Models use partly narrow, non-transferable procedures.
numbers: Example: parseable programs from GPT-3.5 drop from 99% default to 62%, 71%, 75% for vertically flipped, 90-degree and 180-degree rotated drawing settings. Arithmetic better in bases 8 and 16 than 9 and 11 (more common bases).
limits: Counterfactual worlds are only relatively unfamiliar; chain-of-thought and 1-shot help partly but do not close the gap.
agent_relevance: When a task rule differs from the common one, state the rule explicitly and verify with code; do not assume a familiar procedure transfers.

source: Ellis et al. (2020) DreamCoder: wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: A working language-of-thought-style learner: it grows a library of symbolic abstractions and trains a neural search guide, solving tasks by writing programs. It rediscovers functional programming idioms and physics laws.
numbers: Program-synthesis competition set (SyGuS): 3.7% solved before learning, 79.6% after, 40 s average; best competitor CVC4 82.4%; with generous compute 84.3%. Graphics and tower building: others never above 60% held-out, DreamCoder nearly 100%. After 8 cycles it learns 93% of laws and identities tested (as read).
limits: Task domains are small and hand-specified with a seed primitive set.
agent_relevance: Suggests a library-building loop that stores reusable sub-procedures between problems. Out of scope for the current schema; note for the future.

source: Fodor (1975) The Language of Thought
finding: Founding statement: learning and decision theories in cognitive psychology presuppose an internal representational medium with a language-like syntax and semantics.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened; cited from background knowledge.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Fodor and Pylyshyn (1988) Connectionism and cognitive architecture: a critical analysis (original paper)
finding: Original paper: classical architectures have constituent structure and structure-sensitive processes; they predict systematicity, productivity, compositionality and inferential coherence; plain connectionist nets would not.
numbers: No empirical numbers; argument paper.
limits: Not opened this session (open PDF not reachable; web search budget exhausted).
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Fodor and McLaughlin (1990) Connectionism and the problem of systematicity
finding: Argues that Smolensky tensor-product vectors do not have causally operative constituents, so they do not explain systematicity.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened; position as summarised in SEP (a05).
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Smolensky (1988, 1990) Proper treatment of connectionism; tensor product representations
finding: Tensor-product binding of role and filler vectors gives distributed representations with recoverable compositional structure.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened. Later neural-symbolic work not covered here.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Marcus (1998, 2001) Rethinking eliminative connectionism; The Algebraic Mind
finding: Marcus argues that connectionist nets fail to generalise rules outside the training space, whereas humans (including infants) show rule-like generalisation.
numbers: No numbers asserted (not opened).
limits: Not opened; Lake and Baroni 2018 is the modern form of his test.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Piantadosi, Tenenbaum, Goodman (2012, 2016) Bayesian language of thought models of concept learning
finding: Concept learning modelled as Bayesian inference over short programs in a compositional logical language; predicts human learning curves.
numbers: No numbers asserted (not opened).
limits: Not opened. Probabilistic programming is covered in a parallel subfield.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Quilty-Dunn, Porot, Mandelbaum (2023) The best game in town: re-emergence of LOT across cognitive sciences (BBS)
finding: Argues LOT is the best explanation of a cluster of effects (discrete constituents, predicate-argument structure, logical operators, abstract content) across vision, memory, animal and infant cognition. Only the SEP citation was seen.
numbers: No numbers asserted (not opened).
limits: Not opened; SEP lists it as forthcoming in BBS.
